entry.title: RC3-2020: X-ray free electron lasers: A new paradigm in science

media:group.media:title: RC3-2020: X-ray free electron lasers: A new paradigm in science
media:group.media:description:
Presentation by Prof. Dr. Robert Feidenhans’l, Managing Director at European XFEL.
New research opportunities, a flood of scientific data and the future of data storage
More than 60 years ago Rosalind Franklin’s X-ray image of DNA helped solve the structure of this important molecule. Today scientists at the world's largest laser, European XFEL, generate thousands of images every second. This data is used to unravel the structures and movements of viruses, nanoparticles, plasmas and magnetic materials. How do researchers store and analyse petabytes of data arriving at a rate of thousands of frames a second? And how could basic research into magnetism and materials pave the way to new data storage media for the future?

entry.title: RC3-2021: Howto grok an experiment at an FEL

media:group.media:title: RC3-2021: Howto grok an experiment at an FEL
media:group.media:description:
Presentation by James Wrigley, Software Developer for High-Performance Data Analysis at European XFEL.
The European XFEL is the latest generation of light sources. It can generate up to 27,000 extremely short and intense X-ray light pulses which are used to address scientific challenges, such as unveiling the atomic structures of viruses. Each experiment can generate hundreds of terabytes or even petabytes of data, and in this talk we'll discuss the challenges of storing and analyzing that data.
Licensed to the public under http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0

entry.title: 39c3: The Eyes of Photon Science: Imaging, Simulation and the Quest to Make the Invisible Visible

media:group.media:title: 39c3: The Eyes of Photon Science: Imaging, Simulation and the Quest to Make the Invisible Visible
media:group.media:description:
Presentation by Dr. Markus Kuster, Senior Scientist Detector Simulation and Research and Development of Detector Technology.
Science advances by extending our senses beyond the limits of human perception, pushing the boundaries of what we can observe. In photon science, imaging detectors serve as the eyes of science, translating invisible processes into measurable and analysable data. Behind every image lies a deep understanding of how detectors see, respond and perform.
At facilities like the European XFEL, the world's most powerful X-ray free-electron laser located in the Hamburg metropolitan area, imaging detectors capture ultrashort X-ray flashes at MHz frame rates and with high dynamic range. Without these advanced detectors, even the brightest X-ray laser beam would remain invisible. They help to reveal what would otherwise stay hidden, such as the structure of biomolecules, the behaviour of novel materials, and matter under extreme conditions. But how do we know they will perform as expected? And how do we design systems capable of “seeing” the invisible?
I will take a closer look how imaging technology in large-scale facilities is simulated and designed to make the invisible visible. From predicting detector performance to evaluating image quality, we look at how performance simulation helps scientists and engineers understand the “eyes” of modern science.
X-ray imaging detectors have come a long way in the last 15 years, turning ideas that once seemed impossible into realities. Imaging detectors in photon science are more than just high-speed cameras. They are complex systems operating at the limits of what’s physically measurable. Understanding how they behave before, during, and after experiments is essential to advancing both the technology and the science it enables.
In this talk, I’ll take you inside the world of detector simulation and performance modelling. I’ll explore how tools like Monte Carlo simulations, sensor response models, and system-level performance evaluations are used to:
- Predict detector behaviour in extreme conditions (such as MHz X-ray bursts), and - identify critical performance bottlenecks before production.
By linking imaging technology with simulation and modelling, we can better interpret experimental data and design the next generation of scientific cameras. Beyond the technical aspects, this talk reflects on the broader theme of how we “see” though technology, what it means to make the invisible visible, and how simulation changes not only how we build instruments, but also how we understand them.
Licensed to the public under http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0

entry.title: Unraveling the photocycle dynamics of a marine orange carotenoid protein at European XFEL

media:group.media:title: Unraveling the photocycle dynamics of a marine orange carotenoid protein at European XFEL
media:group.media:description: Maria Agustina Dominguez Martin from the University of Córdoba in Spain studies how organisms adapt to changing light conditions with the help of photosensory proteins. Her research focuses on photosynthetic organisms, which harness energy from sunlight. To protect themselves from damage caused by excessive exposure, they rely on a process known as photoprotection. In cyanobacteria, the Orange Carotenoid Protein (OCP) acts as a kind of light-activated switch, helping regulate this process. At the SPB/SFX instrument at European XFEL, Martin and her collaborators recently took a closer look at Synechococcus sp. WH7803, a marine cyanobacterium with distinctive properties, to gain a better understanding of how these organisms protect themselves from excess light in dynamic marine environments.

entry.title: Razor sharp X-ray light produced by the X-Ray Free-Electron Laser Oscillator (XFELO)

media:group.media:title: Razor sharp X-ray light produced by the X-Ray Free-Electron Laser Oscillator (XFELO)
media:group.media:description: Interview with Dr. Harald Sinn (Head of Instrumentation Department, European XFEL) and Dr. Patrick Rauer (Postdoctoral Researcher, DESY) about the new XFELO. For the first time, researchers have amplified X-ray light multiple times in a resonator cavity, in a way highly similar to traditional lasers. With great success: the new technique delivers extremely energetic X-ray pulses for high-precision experiments. This development is called XFELO and opens up entirely new possibilities for research in physics, chemistry, or biology. Researchers from European XFEL, DESY and Hamburg University have published their findings in the journal Nature.

media:group.media:title: XFELO animation
media:group.media:description: The XFELO cavity is 66 metres long, with diamond mirrors at each end. When an electron bunch passes through the alternating magnetic fields of the undulator, it emits an X-ray pulse. This light pulse is then reflected back to meet the next electron bunch less than half a microsecond later. After just a few iterations, the result is an increasingly sharp X-ray pulse that narrows in on one particular wavelength, much like a laser in the visible spectrum. (Music: Light Touch by Podington Bear is licensed under a Attribution-NonCommercial 3.0 International License. https://freemusicarchive.org/music/Podington_Bear/Thoughtful/LightTouch)

media:group.media:title: XFELO-Animation
media:group.media:description: Der Resonator des XFELO ist 66 Meter lang und ist an beiden Enden mit Diamantspiegeln ausgestattet. Wenn ein Elektronenbündel die abwechselnd gepolten Magnetfelder des Undulators durchläuft, sendet es einen Röntgenpuls aus. Dieser Lichtpuls wird reflektiert und trifft weniger als eine halbe Mikrosekunde später auf das nächste Elektronenbündel. Nach nur wenigen Durchläufen entsteht ein immer schärferer Röntgenpuls, der sich auf eine bestimmte Wellenlänge verengt, ähnlich wie ein Laser im sichtbaren Spektrum. entry.title: The new HXS beamline at European XFEL

media:group.media:title: The new HXS beamline at European XFEL
media:group.media:description: The HXS (High-Energy X-ray Scattering) instrument will be the third experiment at the SASE2 undulator beamline, complementing the existing MID and HED instruments. The main construction work was completed during the long facility maintenance period in the second half of 2025. In the XTD6 photon tunnel, a 500 m beam-transport section was installed to deliver the European XFEL beam to HXS. A major challenge was the limited clearance to the tunnel wall over several hundred meters, which required custom-designed support structures for the beam-transport pipes. In the experiment hall, a dedicated hutch—including a control room and two rack rooms—was constructed. The key challenge here was integrating the new infrastructure into the existing MID and HED hutch layout while maintaining functional transport routes and compliant escape paths. With the basic infrastructure now in place, several smaller components—such as an X-ray mirror and a photon shutter—will be installed during 2026. First beam in the HXS hutch is expected in early 2027. From 2027 onward, the HXS beam transport and hutch will be used to develop beam-sharing techniques and to advance X-ray optics, diagnostics, and detectors for high photon energies. Scientific experiments will then be prepared and carried out with a focus on photon energies from 15 keV to 60 keV, making use of the new superconducting undulators that will be commissioned in parallel.

entry.title: Making X‑ray flashes visible: MHz X‑ray Imaging with Hybrid Pixel Detectors at the European XFEL

media:group.media:title: Making X‑ray flashes visible: MHz X‑ray Imaging with Hybrid Pixel Detectors at the European XFEL
media:group.media:description:
Hybrid pixel detectors are the “eyes” of photon science at the European XFEL, turning ultrashort X‑ray flashes into precise, analysable images. Built for extreme conditions, they capture data at MHz image frame rates while delivering very low noise and a very high dynamic range, so that even single photons and the brightest X‑ray laser pulses become measurable at the same time.
A key strength of hybrid pixel detectors is their working principle, the detector combines two functional layers. In the top layer, the sensor, incoming X‑ray photons generate an electrical charge in the semiconductor. This charge is collected pixel by pixel and passed directly to a dedicated readout chip (application-specific integrated circuit, ASIC), the bottom layer. The ASIC chip is connected to the sensor using microscopic metallic contacts (bump‑bonds). The ASIC provides each pixel with its own electronics to amplify, process, buffer, and transfer the signal, enabling fast and reliable imaging even when intensities change rapidly from pulse to pulse. As such, hybrid pixel technology integrates both sensor and readout electronics in one highly integrated device.
With hybrid pixel detectors, the European XFEL expands what researchers can observe, from biomolecular structures and novel materials to matter under extreme conditions, making the invisible visible with high precision and speed.

entry.title: Superconducting undulator technology at European XFEL

media:group.media:title: Superconducting undulator technology at European XFEL
media:group.media:description: European XFEL is developing superconducting undulators (SCUs) to boost magnetic field strength at short periods, enabling brighter beams, broader tunability, and access to very hard X‑rays. This technology represents a major leap in producing high-quality X-ray beams. The superconducting magnets generate intense, coherent X-ray pulses with unprecedented brightness and tunability. The development is progressing well, with successful design implementations that minimize energy loss while maximizing efficiency. This technology enhances the XFEL’s capabilities, allowing researchers to investigate complex structures and dynamic processes across materials science, chemistry, and biology with greater precision. Moreover, the undulator's tunability allows for a broad spectrum of X-ray wavelengths, opening new avenues for scientific inquiry.

entry.title: Studying foams and the interior of planets with HED HIBEF

media:group.media:title: Studying foams and the interior of planets with HED HIBEF
media:group.media:description: With the two powerful lasers of HED HIBEF Alejandro Laso Garcia from Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR) tests a special imaging method and a new setup for small-angle X-ray scattering*. He is especially interested in the study of foams. But the knowledge and experience he gains will also be very valuable for future beamtime. At HED HIBEF you can as well create very extreme conditions, like in the interior of the Sun, the Earth or other planets. And experiments like that can also help to understand processes like nuclear fusion. * HIBEF stands for Helmholtz International Beamline for Extreme Fields

entry.title: Understanding and controlling proton transfer in water

media:group.media:title: Understanding and controlling proton transfer in water
media:group.media:description: Determining the key mechanisms underlying solvent-mediated proton transfer is essential for the understanding acidbase reactions. Femtosecond spectroscopic experiments and quantum chemical molecular dynamics calculations have shown the characteristic femtosecond to picosecond time scales for elementary proton transfer events. Until now experimental studies have determined possible proton transfer pathways without revealing the role of electronic structural changes of acids and bases. We aim to decipher the electronic structural dynamics of the frontier orbitals of imidazole as a base model system using femtosecond N K-edge RIXS, using a photoacid to optically trigger the reaction. This will enable us to indentify how electronic structural changes steer the proton to follow particular pathways and the possible outcome of the reaction. Our findings will contribute to refine the current understanding of proton transfer in e.g. hydrogen fuel cells and transmembrane protein proton pumps.

media:group.media:title: Chiral molecules in polarised light
media:group.media:description: Markus Ilchen from the University of Hamburg and Arno Ehresmann from the University of Kassel are investigating at the SQS instrument of European XFEL how polarised light knocks electrons out of chiral molecules. Chiral molecules have both a “left” and a “right” configuration – just as we have a left and a right hand. Depending on the polarisation of the X-ray light, the electrons are ejected in different directions, especially if there are electrical charges at certain points in the molecule. In their experiment, the team investigated gaseous methyloxirane (C3H6O). It is used for dyes, flavourings, antioxidants, emulsifiers and enzymes, among other things. The measurement with the X-ray flashes of European XFEL is so fast that the atoms of the molecule do not have time to move. This allows to investigate the pure influence of the charges.

entry.title: Aerosols in X-ray light at European XFEL

media:group.media:title: Aerosols in X-ray light at European XFEL
media:group.media:description: Nano- to micrometer sized particles and droplets in air, known as aerosols, play a decisive role in the formation of clouds, for the climate of Earth, for air quality and for human health. However, many processes have not yet been researched in detail. At the SPB/SFX instrument of European XFEL, Nønne Prisle and her team from the University of Oulu, Finland, are therefore investigating artificial aerosol mixtures and their interaction with water vapour, which is omnipresent in the atmosphere. The extraordinarily high intensity of the X-ray flashes from European XFEL and their high repetition rate allow precise small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) in combination with single particle imaging (SPI). The results could have far-reaching implications for the fundamental understanding of atmospheric aerosols and their impact on the global climate.
